tagline: Through cotton valleys and forest, the road climbs to a mountaintop river.
intro: The Appalachian Highlands Scenic Byway winds through northeastern Alabama’s forests and cotton country before climbing Lookout Mountain and descending into Fort Payne. Alabama Byways lists this state byway as approximately 80 miles between I-20 near Heflin and I-59 at Fort Payne. Its account emphasizes mountain scenery, geologic formations and historic rural communities, calling Little River Canyon National Preserve the route’s highlight.

Railroads helped shape the towns connected by the drive. The Selma, Rome, and Dalton Railroad reached Piedmont in 1868; the town grew during the industrial boom that followed. Another former rail corridor now carries walkers and cyclists: the Seaboard/CSX line became the Chief Ladiga Trail, which the byway crosses in Piedmont. Rail connections between Birmingham and Chattanooga also stimulated Fort Payne’s growth, while its late-1880s coal-and-iron boom brought investors and workers from New England and the North.

From Heflin, follow US 78 and AL 9 west through Talladega National Forest, then AL 9 north through White Plains and Choccolocco State Forest, along the Dugger Mountain Scenic Drive toward Piedmont. Cotton fields accompany the route through Ellisville toward Centre; US 411 then leads west to Leesburg. AL 273 heads northeast through mountain valleys to Blanche, where AL 35 climbs Lookout Mountain, crosses the preserve and descends to Fort Payne.

moments.title: Piedmont
moments.text: Piedmont’s railroad connections now include a place to walk or cycle: the former Seaboard/CSX corridor became the Chief Ladiga Trail through downtown. The community began at the crossroads of two early post roads and was known as Hollow Stump and Cross Plains before residents chose Piedmont in 1888. The Selma, Rome, and Dalton Railroad had arrived in 1868. At the Southern Railroad Depot Museum, displays tell the town’s story; a caboose sits beside the original loading dock and cargo cart. Victorian-era and early-20th-century houses surround downtown, where commercial buildings, churches and schools date from the first half of the 20th century.

moments.title: Little River Canyon
moments.text: Little River flows along the middle of Lookout Mountain for almost its entire length, cutting a canyon before leaving the mountain for Weiss Lake. Sandstone cliffs rise as much as 600 feet above the narrow canyon floor. The byway crosses the preserve on AL 35; the separate Canyon Rim Parkway follows the western rim, where cliffs are frequently visible. Congress created the national preserve in 1992. Little River Falls marks the beginning of the canyon, a feature Alabama Byways singles out among the area’s sightseeing highlights. The rim road’s northern half was built under federal supervision during the New Deal; local authorities built its southern half.

moments.title: Fort Payne
moments.text: Fort Payne’s late-1880s coal-and-iron boom brought investors and workers, but the deposits proved smaller than expected and the town entered an economic decline. A different industry followed: the W.B. Davis Hosiery Mill began making socks and hosiery from area cotton in 1907. By the beginning of the 21st century, the local hosiery industry produced more than half the socks made in the United States. The Main Street Historic District reflects a later phase of growth, with utilitarian brick commercial buildings and the Art Moderne City Hall of 1941. The district’s civic buildings also include the 1936 Classical Revival Post Office, adding a different architectural treatment to its commercial streets.
